title: Cinder's Loop

pages.text:
*Sky Report: bright, blustery, a good day to be looked at.*

The Windmill Fields lay flat and golden, the blades turning with a slow, wooden groan. The air smelled of dry stalks and hot dust. Pip and Nettle perched on a low fence rail, their toes gripping the rough wood. Below them, the Trial entrants practiced in tight formations.

Cinder led them. He was a blur of glossy chestnut, his wings beating with a power that made the air shimmer. He spiraled upward, trailing a line of younger sparrows who struggled to keep pace. The spiral was perfect, unbroken, a continuous line of motion against the blue. The whole hedge, gathered on the hedgerow behind the fence, cheered until their throats ached.

Pip’s wings twitched against her sides. The itch was a physical thing, a tingling heat in her shoulder blades. She looked at the sky, then at her own small, brown body. She looked at the wind, which was pushing gently against her flank.

"He does it with his muscles," Nettle whispered, her eyes wide. "I do it with my eyes. What do you do?"

Pip tilted her head. The wind ruffled her crooked tail feather. "I listen," she said.

The cheer from the hedge rose again, a wave of sound that hit her chest. Her heart beat fast and hard, a tiny drum in a small body.
pages.image: A tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail feather sits on a wooden fence rail watching a large chestnut sparrow spiral high above a field of golden wheat under a bright blue sky.

pages.text:
A shadow dropped over them. Cinder landed on the fence post, his weight making the wood creak. He preened his chestnut feathers, looking down at the two small sparrows with a grin that was all beak and no kindness.

"Did you hear that, small one?" he called out, his voice carrying to the watching flock. "Pip is here to be a windmill. She wants to spin."

The hedge laughed. It was a sharp, quick laugh, the kind that starts in the throat and pops out before you can stop it. Cinder hopped closer, his big eyes bright with amusement.

"Come on," he said, spreading his wings wide. "One loop. Just one. Let’s see if you can fly a circle or if you’ll just fall."

Pip looked at Nettle. Nettle shrank into herself, her big feet gripping the rail. Pip looked at the wind. The wind was high, pushing hard from the west, not the gentle breeze of the morning. It was a strong, tricky wind. She knew she would fail. She knew her wings were too short for this.

But if she stayed on the fence, she would never know how the wind felt when it tried to break her.

"Watch closely," Pip said.

She pushed off the rail.
pages.image: A large, arrogant chestnut sparrow stands on a fence post looking down at a tiny, nervous brown sparrow with a crooked tail feather, while a crowd of sparrows watches from a nearby hedge.

pages.text:
She hit the air and immediately lost her balance. The wind slapped her side, hard and cold, and her wings flailed in a panic. She tried to steer, to fight the gust, but she was too light, too small. The air pushed her into a lopsided tumble. She spun, the ground rushing up to meet her, and she dropped twenty feet in a single breath.

The hedge gasped, then roared with laughter. Pip crashed into a patch of thistles, the spines pricking her soft belly. She lay there, trembling, her face hot with shame. The thorns were sharp and angry.

Then she heard Tuck’s voice, dry and quiet in her memory. *Don’t fight it. Ride it.*

She stopped thrashing. She stopped trying to push against the wind. She spread her wings wide, flat, and let the air lift them. The gust that had thrown her now caught her underside. Her body rose, not straight up, but in a long, curving arc, sliding along the invisible current. The thistles fell away. The fence went up.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow with a crooked tail feather tumbles downward through the air towards a patch of prickly thistles while a crowd of sparrows on a fence watches in shock.

pages.text:
Not a loop. A spiral. An unlikely, rising curl that she hadn’t planned. The wind caught her, lifted her, and carried her higher. She climbed above the mill, above the fence, above the heads of the laughing birds. She hung there, effortless and shining, her wings held steady while the air did the work.

The laughter died. The hedge went silent. Pip was a speck of brown against the blue, turning slowly in the updraft. It looked like the tiniest, strangest, loveliest kind of flying. It looked like a dandelion seed refusing to land.

Nettle let out a whoop that was half shout, half squeak. "Pip! Look at her!"

Pip felt the wind change, softer now, and she angled her body to glide down. She was not fighting. She was dancing. The air held her, and she held the air. For a moment, she was not the smallest sparrow in the hedge. She was the only one in the sky.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow hangs high in the air above a windmill, spinning slowly in a gentle updraft while a large crowd of sparrows on a fence looks up in awe.

pages.text:
Pip landed on the fence rail, her legs shaking so hard she could barely stand. She puffed her chest out, trying to look calm, but her tail feather was still twitching. Cinder was still on the post, his beak slightly open. He squinted at her, his expression stiff and confused.

"Lucky gust," he said. His voice was flat, stripped of its usual swagger.

Pip looked at him. Then she looked at the wind, which was blowing gently across the field.

"Maybe," she said. "But it was my gust."

She turned and flew off, Nettle buzzing at her side. They disappeared over the hedge, leaving the field behind. In the shadows of a nearby hawthorn, a large chestnut shape watched them go. Cinder’s eyes were dark and serious. He was not laughing any more. He was thinking.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow with a crooked tail feather flies away from a fence while a large, serious-looking chestnut sparrow watches from the shadows of a leafy bush.
